title: Mercy in power
hook: the rulers people still speak of warmly are remembered for mercy

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ordinary believer: the sweeper of the mosque, and the mothers, farmers and traders who carried the faith. Your line was ordinary hands carried it. Who did you thank? Day one thousand fifty-one.

A parent at bedtime. A shift manager writing next week's schedule. A teacher holding a red pen over a failing paper. A referee with a whistle. A landlord reading a late-rent text. None of them is a sultan. All of them hold a little power over someone else, and every day they choose how to use it. This path has walked past a lot of rulers this year. Some built, some conquered, some fell. When you ask which of them people still speak of warmly, a pattern shows up, and it isn't the size of the army. Today: mercy in power.
screen: `A PARENT, A MANAGER, A REFEREE.` → `EVERYONE HOLDS A LITTLE POWER.` → `WHICH RULERS ARE SPOKEN OF WARMLY?`

segments.voice: Go back to two names from earlier this year. Salah al-Din, who retook Jerusalem and let its people ransom themselves and leave, instead of putting the city to the sword. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, who began his reforms with his own family's wealth. Neither story is told today for the size of an army. What people still retell is the mercy. Second, the Qur'an puts mercy at the root of leadership. After the battle of Uhud, when some of the Prophet's companions had failed him, a verse speaks to him, in Pickthall's translation: "It was by the mercy of Allah that thou wast lenient with them (O Muhammad), for if thou hadst been stern and fierce of heart they would have dispersed from round about thee." And then, in the same verse, it tells him to pardon them, to ask forgiveness for them, and to consult them. Not to punish. To keep them close and keep listening. Third, a hadith brings this down to every household. In Sahih al-Bukhari the Prophet, peace be upon him, says each of you is a shepherd, and each is responsible for the flock: the ruler for his people, a man for his family, a woman for her husband's household, a servant for what his master left in his care. Small power is still power. Fourth, another hadith, in Jami' at-Tirmidhi: the merciful are shown mercy by the Most Merciful. Be merciful to those on earth, and the One above will be merciful to you. The red pen, the schedule, the whistle. Each one a small throne. And the history suggests what will be remembered from it.
screen: `SALAH AL-DIN AND UMAR: THE MERCY IS TOLD.` · `LENIENT, OR THEY WOULD HAVE SCATTERED.` · `EACH OF YOU IS A SHEPHERD.` · `THE MERCIFUL ARE SHOWN MERCY.` · then, large: `IT WAS BY THE MERCY OF ALLAH.`

segments.voice: The practice: use your small power mercifully. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself one honest question: where do I hold a little power over someone? A child, an employee, a student, a younger sibling, a person waiting on a reply from you. Pick one. Picture them. Now picture the next moment you'll have a choice about them: a mistake to correct, a request to answer, a deadline to enforce. Don't drop the standard. Just see what a lenient answer would look like, the kind that keeps them close. Rest there until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Mercy in power. Leniency and pardon from the one who could punish, the thing people remember of their rulers. Today's word.
Your line: mercy is remembered. Today, when your small power meets someone's mistake, answer one notch gentler than you planned. Day one thousand fifty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims often cite the hadith that each person is a shepherd responsible for a flock, and the Qur'an's praise of the Prophet's leniency, when speaking about how parents, employers and leaders should treat those in their care.

fork.setup: you lead a community. at a critical moment some of your people left their posts, and it cost dearly. now they're back in front of you. what do you do?
options: make an example of them, so it never happens again.
pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and keep consulting them.
forgive them quietly, but stop asking their advice.
fork.reveal: Qur'an 3:159, after Uhud, praises the Prophet's leniency and tells him to pardon them, ask forgiveness for them, and consult them in the affair.

trapdoor: what you thought: mercy is for saints, and power is for rulers.
what it means: mercy is what people remember from those who held power, large or small.
what a scholar hears: 3:159 ties the community's survival to the Prophet's leniency after Uhud, and the shepherd hadith in Bukhari gives every household its own small rule.

sources.quoted: It was by the mercy of Allah that thou wast lenient with them (O Muhammad), for if thou hadst been stern and fierce of heart they would have dispersed from round about thee.

notes: Pickthall 3:159 quoted from memory (matches wording used elsewhere on this path); confirm. The rest of the verse (pardon, ask forgiveness, consult) is paraphrased.
The setting of 3:159 after Uhud follows the classical commentaries; confirm phrasing 'some of the Prophet's companions had failed him'.
Bukhari 893 and Tirmidhi 1924 paraphrased; confirm numbers.
Salah al-Din (day 957) and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (day 907) are referred back to with the index wording of those days only; no new historical claims.
Index hook says 'the best rulers are remembered for mercy'; the script avoids the superlative and frames it as 'what people still tell'.
Editor: shepherd hadith (Bukhari 893) brought closer to its wording: 'a woman for her husband's household, a servant for his master's property', replacing 'a worker'.

Audit: 'let people ransom out or leave in peace' overstated 1187: leaving was by ransom, and many who could not pay were taken captive (some were freed without ransom). Now 'let its people ransom themselves and leave, instead of putting the city to the sword'; match pair aligned. 'Their battles and budgets are footnotes now' (an unsourced sweep, and Umar II is not known for battles) softened.
